title: Borrowed chord progressions: Tiger Rag, I Got Rhythm and Pom Pom
summary: Carter did little writing on borrowed changes; he used the I Got Rhythm structure in Pom Pom.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, there's another category, too, that --there is another technique that I have given a name to; I'm not going to launch it to that, but that is in which chord progressions were borrowed and then the original melody of that song, or whatever was discarded, and then the jazz arranger would put his own melody to that, borrowed set of chord progressions.
This is something else that it seems to me that you didn't do very much of; in fact, I'm really groping around for examples of that in this period.
I don't think anybody did much of that, did they, before Charlie Parker, I mean, you know?
Well, there was actually ... I mean, Duke did quite a bit of it himself; I mean, he ...

Well, the only instance I can recall is "Rose Room" which became In a Mellow Tone, and I think da da dee da ... what's the name of that? "I Let a Song Out of My Heart"? I understand that came from a lick that saxaphones played to "Once in Awhile"? Is that right?
Umm ... that could be. Uh huh.
Da, doo da da da and da doo dee dee... what else?
Well, there's a number of -- even a number of Ellington pieces.
That's what I mean. What other Ellington's can you ...
A little "Tiger Rag" ... lots of "Tiger Rag" pieces.
Oh, yes ... well, yes.
When the melody was discarded.
Yes. I don't know too many of those, though. Especially by other people, I don't know of any of them.
I don't have a list here, but the Missourians was another group that did a number of those.
Is that right?
Those "Tiger Rag" things -- [the Ozark Mountain groups] and so forth.
Taken from what?
From the chord progressions of "Tiger Rag."
Oh, yes. "Tiger Rag," yeah. Well ...
Well, the Basie band then, with a lot of "I Got Rhythm" ...
Oh yes.
But in general, I mean, is it ...
I even use an "I Got Rhythm" bridge in
a thing of mine called "Pom Pom".
Indeed. That's what? 1940?
Yeah. I mean, it had the "I Got Rhythm" chord structure. You know, and ... of course, I think the "I Got Rhythm" introductory melody first came from something by William Grant Still.
This has been claimed from the Afro American Symphony." This is what some people claim they say.
Yeah, the symphony ...
But I've gone through the score, and I can't find much on it.

Well, maybe it's not the Afro American Symphony." I think it's something earlier than that. And I think it's ... let me see, I can't remember the name of it, but I heard it. I heard it at something played by the Houston Symphony Orchestra when they played a thing -- a TV program, oh, I can't remember the title of it, but I wrote it down somewhere at home.
But in general, I think it's safe to say ...
But what I'm talking about is the part that says, da da da da, dee dee dee ... that's the part I'm talking about.
In the bridge ... at the end of the bridge.
No, not in the bridge. The melody. The da da da ... I got rhythm, da da da ... that's a William Grant Still thing. Definitely. Very definitely.
Okay. Well, I'll await your reference to that.
No, now I didn't mean the bridge on that. No.
Because the bridge in that case ... I mean, there are other songs even earlier than "I Got Rhythm" that had the same chord structure in the bridge, that's right.
Yes, that is right.
But in general, is it a fair statement to say that this is a technique of composing or arranging which you indulged very little? This kind of borrowed chord progression.
Well, I guess maybe I didn't. Maybe I should have.

Because it strikes me, in listening to these things -- well, comparing them, too, to a lot of other people active in various times. But there's a great deal of original material in your work, and maybe not even so many popular songs of the time as there is in other band leaders repertoires.
Never thought of it. Silly of me, wasn't it? Or negligent. Which?
